Describe where things are in a room or in a courtyard.
On Sunday, in the courtyard of the building on Kastanienallee, the party for Fritz is being prepared, Mrs Hoffmann's idea. Lena is in charge, Mara and Piotr carry things.
Right, everyone! Piotr, please put the big table in the middle, under the chestnut tree.
In the middle? But there's still snow there.
Then put it next to the bench, against the wall. It's dry there.
And the chairs? Where shall I put the chairs?
Around the table. And put the blankets on the chairs, it's cold.
Where are the fairy lights? I put them in the cellar yesterday.
They're not in the cellar any more. Ola has already brought them. They're on the stairs, in the box.
Above the table, from the chestnut tree to Grandpa's window. Then they hang right above the food.
And the speaker? Mrs Hoffmann only wants to play the piano, but her piano is on the fourth floor.
I've got an idea. She just opens the window. The courtyard is small, you can hear everything. Like in the old days, Ludwig says.
Perfect! And Fritz? Where is the guest of honour, actually?
He's lying under the table. Next to the sausages. Where else?
stellen = “SHTEL-len” (to put), stehen = “SHTAY-en” (to stand). The difference: short “ll” vs. long “eh”.
legen = “LAY-ghen” (long e), liegen = “LEE-ghen” (long i). Listen to the difference in the vowel!
Nine prepositions can take either the DATIVE or the ACCUSATIVE. It all depends on the question:
Der Tisch steht im Hof. (in dem)
Ich stelle den Tisch in den Hof.
The nine prepositions: in, an, auf, unter, über, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen.
Trick: if you can ask “where to?” (there is movement from one place to another), you use the accusative. If the thing just “is” there, the dative.
“an” vs. “auf”: the lamp is “an der Decke” (on the ceiling, hanging), the book is “auf dem Tisch” (on the table, resting on top). The picture is “an der Wand”.
Contractions: in dem → im, in das → ins, an dem → am, an das → ans, auf das → aufs (informal).
3. Verb pairs: to put / to be

German is very precise: the verb says HOW something stands or how you put an object. The verbs of movement are regular and take the accusative; the verbs of position are irregular and take the dative:
upright objects: bottle, chair, table, piano
objects lying flat: book, blanket, phone, key
I put the bottle on the table. → The bottle is on the table.
I put the phone on the table. → The phone is on the table.
I hang the jacket on the door. → The jacket is hanging on the door.
I sit down on the sofa. → I'm sitting on the sofa.

In English we say “put” and “is” for almost everything. In German you have to choose: a book “liegt” (lies flat), a bottle “steht” (stands upright). A town or a country “liegt”: “Berlin liegt an der Spree”.
4. Prepositions of time with the same words
Some of these prepositions are also used for time, always with the DATIVE:
before the meal, two years ago
I put the table in the courtyard.
The phone is on the table.
Put the phone on the table!
The picture is hanging on the wall.
Fritz is lying under the table.
Ich ___ die Flasche auf den Tisch.
The bottle stands upright + movement → stellen.
The book is lying flat + position → liegen.
Wohin hast du den Schlüssel gelegt?
I hang the fairy lights above the door.
I put the blankets on the chairs.
The table is next to the bench.

Warum stellt er ihn nicht in die Mitte?

By four o'clock in the afternoon everything was ready. The long table stood against the wall, next to the old wooden bench. On the table was Kasia's red-and-white tablecloth, and on it were plates, glasses and two big flasks of mulled wine and hot cocoa for the children.

Above the table hung the fairy lights, from the chestnut tree to Ludwig's window on the first floor. It was still light, but the little bulbs were already glowing. Mara had put a blanket on every chair, and under the table Lena had laid an old rug so that Fritz wouldn't have to lie on the cold ground.

The food came from every flat. Kasia brought pierogi and Polish cake. Lena put three trays of plum cake on the table, even though it wasn't plum season: she had frozen them in the summer. For the first time in Berlin, Mara had made sarmale (Romanian cabbage rolls), from her grandmother's recipe. She put the big pot in the middle of the table and everyone wanted to know what it was.
Sarmale! My mother used to make them too. After the war, when we had nothing. But without meat, just with potatoes.
Mine have meat, rice and lots of love. And you eat them with sour cream and mămăligă. That's a kind of maize porridge.

Ludwig sat at the head of the table, on the best chair. His cast had come off on Thursday, and he kept moving the fingers of his right hand, as if he couldn't believe it. At first Fritz lay on the rug under the table, as planned. But after five minutes he was sitting on Kuba's lap and nobody had seen how he got there.

Jonas and Clara had come too, and even Dr Yılmaz with her guitar. She sat down next to Ludwig and asked him: “Mr Brandt, are you allowed to play yet?” Ludwig grinned: “Doctor, today I'm not asking what I'm allowed to do.”

Dr Yılmaz tasted the sarmale and immediately wanted the recipe. “In Turkey we call them sarma,” she said. “Almost the same word! My mother puts them in the pot like little soldiers, all in a row.” Mara laughed: “So does my grandmother. And she puts the pot in the oven for three hours, not on the hob.” Kasia called from the other end of the table: “In Poland they're called gołąbki. That means little pigeons!” Jonas looked into the pot and said: “Well, I don't see any pigeons in here. Just very good food.”

It got dark. The fairy lights now sparkled above their heads, and the little bulbs were reflected in the mulled wine. Then, at six o'clock, a window opened up on the fourth floor. Everyone looked up. Mrs Hoffmann was standing at the window in a dark blue dress, waving.
I've pushed my piano to the window! Well, not me. Piotr pushed it this morning. The first song is for Fritz!

And then the music came down from the fourth floor, through the open window, into the little courtyard. First something cheerful, a fast waltz, and the twins danced between the chairs. Then a song everyone knew. Ludwig picked up his guitar, Dr Yılmaz hers, and they played along too, down in the courtyard, while the piano played up above.

Slowly other windows opened as well. Not only in their building, but also in the buildings to the left and right of the courtyard. A young man on the third floor opposite put a candle on his windowsill. An old woman on the ground floor brought out a chair and sat in front of her door with a blanket over her knees. A student put his headphones aside and listened.
Ludwig, look. The whole street is listening.
It was always like this in the old days. In summer, with the windows open. Margarete played, and all the courtyards were quiet. Back then we didn't have a television. We had Margarete.

At the end, Mrs Hoffmann played a quiet piece, very softly. Nobody spoke. Even the twins sat quietly on the bench, with Fritz between them. When the last note faded away in the courtyard, there was a moment of complete silence. Then everyone clapped, in the courtyard and at the windows, and from somewhere someone shouted: “Encore!”
Mrs Hoffmann leaned out of the window. Mara saw that she was laughing, just like in the old photo from the Konzerthaus.
An encore? With pleasure! But then somebody has to bring me a mulled wine up to the fourth floor!

Kuba jumped up, grabbed a mug and ran up the stairs, three steps at a time. Fritz ran after him. Ludwig watched them go and said, more to himself than to Mara: “A courtyard, a piano, a few neighbours. You don't really need more than that.”
